slides.0.title: Climate Change and the Future of Portuguese Wine
slides.0.subtitle: Level 4 · Environmental Challenges and Strategies
slides.0.points.0.label: The 1.5°C Reality
slides.0.points.0.text: Alentejo in southern Portugal is already one of the fastest-warming areas in Europe
slides.0.points.1.label: Grape variety shift
slides.0.points.1.text: Demand is rising for heat-tolerant varieties, and northern regions (Minho, Vinho Verde) benefit
slides.0.points.2.label: Altitude and latitude
slides.0.points.2.text: High-altitude vineyards and the Atlantic coast in the west become future refuges
slides.1.title: Climate Challenges Facing Portugal
slides.1.html:
📈 Observed Changes (1990–2024)

  • Average temperatures up 1.2–1.8°C: the largest rise is in the southern Alentejo, bringing harvest dates forward by 2–3 weeks
  • Increasing drought frequency: five severe droughts hit southern Portugal between 2004 and 2023
  • Extreme heatwaves: the 2003, 2017 and 2022 heatwaves caused uneven over-ripeness
  • Irregular rainfall: the total may not fall, but it is more concentrated in autumn and winter, and summers are drier

🍷 Specific Effects on Wine

  • Rising alcohol (12.5% → 13.5–14.5%): grape sugar accumulates faster
  • Falling acidity: affects ageing potential and freshness
  • Flavours shift towards riper, jammier notes, with less of the traditional floral and mineral character
  • Compressed harvest windows: faster decisions are needed
slides.2.title: Climate Change Impact and Response by Region
slides.2.items.0.label: Alentejo (high impact)
slides.2.items.0.desc: The most vulnerable. Summer heat combined with drought. Responses: night harvesting, irrigation, seeking high-altitude plots, heat-tolerant varieties
slides.2.items.1.label: Vinho Verde (beneficiary)
slides.2.items.1.desc: Its cool Atlantic climate makes it a refuge from warming. Alvarinho stays fresh despite rising temperatures, and demand is growing
slides.2.items.2.label: Douro (medium impact)
slides.2.items.2.desc: High-altitude vineyards cushion the impact. Challenge: the Douro Superior becoming too hot. Opportunity: improved quality from high-altitude Douro plots
slides.2.items.3.label: Madeira (special case)
slides.2.items.3.desc: The island climate is relatively stable, but a trend towards tropical conditions makes it harder for white grapes (Sercial) to keep their acidity
slides.3.title: Climate Adaptation Strategies of Portuguese Producers
slides.3.html:
🌿 Viticultural Techniques

  • Raising vine height (tall Lyre or Vertical Shoot Positioning) to increase canopy shade and lower bunch temperature
  • Delayed pruning: delays budburst and pushes harvest later, avoiding the hottest period
  • Precision irrigation: drip irrigation is widely used in Alentejo; the Douro traditionally has no irrigation, but regulations are gradually relaxing
  • Cover crops (cover crop): reduce soil evaporation and regulate root-zone temperature

🍇 Grape Diversification Strategies

  • Rediscovering heat- and drought-tolerant native old varieties: Alicante Bouschet, Moreto, Manteúdo
  • Alvarinho moving north: extending from Minho to more regions
  • Adjusting planting: choosing cooler aspects (north-facing slopes) and higher-altitude plots

🏔️ Geographic Relocation

The Serra da Estrela mountains, the inland highlands of Beira Interior and the northernmost Vinho Verde sub-region of Monção e Melgaço are becoming climate refuges, attracting investment.
slides.4.question: In the face of climate change, which Portuguese region is considered a "beneficiary" because its cool Atlantic climate makes it a refuge?
slides.4.explanation: Vinho Verde lies in north-west Portugal, most strongly influenced by the Atlantic, with relatively cool temperatures. As global warming makes the southern regions ever hotter, Vinho Verde's freshness is increasingly favoured by the market, especially Alvarinho white wines.
